newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS - Renault defends closure, unions call stoppage.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Renault defends closure, unions call stoppage.

text.p: Renault chairman Louis Schweitzer, sticking firmly by plans to close the French carmaker's Belgian plant as trade unions called a one-hour protest strike in three countries, said on Friday the move was traumatic but necessary.
"It's a brutal, hard and painful decision," Schweitzer told Europe 1 radio on a day when unions have called one-hour protest strikes at Renault SA plants in Belgium, France and Spain.
"It's a trauma which I understand, a trauma which I believe necessary," he said of the decision announced last week to close the Belgian Vilvoorde plant with the loss of 3,100 jobs.
The decision has provoked a storm of protest beyond the trade union movement, including condemnation by Belgian Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene, whose political base is Vilvoorde.

European Commissioner Karel Van Miert, a Belgian Socialist, said on Thursday he was blocking state subsidies to a Renault plant in Spain, saying it was "absurd" that the firm close a profitable plant while investing with government aid in Spain.

French Prime Minister Alain Juppe has asked Schweitzer to meet Belgian staff representatives as soon as possible and a a meeting of the company's European works council of employers and worker representatives has been set for next Tuesday in Paris, a day unions are planning a further demonstration.
"I hope these 3,100 people will find another job...that they will continue to make their living, with others or with other Renault factories in France," Schweitzer said.
The Renault boss said the decision had to be taken to secure the future of the company and that, now that it was taken, he hoped for a dialogue with unions.
"They're not yet at the stage where they accept a dialogue," he said, stressing the closure decision was "my responsibility" alone. "The reality is harsh, but it's the reality," he said.
"If we do nothing the company will die," he said.
"European growth, car sector growth is slow," he said adding that securing Renault's growth depended on tapping into "markets other than European ones".

"There will be other cuts in staff in France but there will not be other restructuring plans between now and the year 2000 because we have, in the wake of the Vilvoorde decision, an industrial balance," he added.
Renault has already said 2,700 job losses in France are also in the pipeline.

Asked if the French government, still a shareholder to the tune of 46 percent in Renault, had any intention of moving to push him out of his post, Schweitzer replied, "not that I know" and added that he himself was not planning any such move.

Although Renault's shares soared in the wake of the plant closure announcement last Thursday, they have suffered since as investors who warmed to the plan initially began to worry about whether the political risk could stop it coming to fruition.
Renault shares opened lower on the Paris bourse and were trading 2.36 percent at 136.5 francs in the minutes after the stock exchange opened.
